topic: Stage 2 status and specifications
question: I refer to stage 2 of the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project, and I ask: (a) What is the status of stage 2 of the project; (b) Is stage 2 still intended to proceed; (c) If yes to (b), when is stage 2 expected to proceed; and (d) What are the specifications of stage 2, including: (i) the number of additional beds; (ii) the type of each bed; and (iii) additional security measures?
answer_full:
(a-d)

The State Government has engaged ADCO Constructions (ADCO) under the Early Contractor Involvement (ECI) process to progress the Graylands Campus Project, including 32 new sub-acute male forensic mental health beds, an eight-bed child and adolescent forensic mental health unit and an Integrated Patient Services and Rehabilitation Centre.

Future announcements will be made in due course.
so_what: Confirms what Stage 1 actually is — 32 sub-acute beds, an 8-bed child and adolescent unit, and a rehab centre — with ADCO now formally engaged. Stage 2 is not addressed at all: no status, no timing, no bed numbers, just "future announcements in due course." The campus's full end state remains undefined and uncommitted beyond Stage 1.

topic: Project webpage not updated since April 2025
question: I refer to the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project webpage on the Mental Health Commission website, and I ask: (a) What is the name of the role of the person responsible for maintaining this page; (b) What other responsibilities does the role under (a) have; and (c) Why was it last updated on 22 April 2025, given the developments since?
answer_full:
(A) There is no one role responsible for maintaining this page. Commissioning and Programs provide information and Strategic Communications update website.

(B) N/A.

(C) The page referred to on the Mental Health Commission website is about the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensic Taskforce which concluded its term in July 2023.

This webpage has a last updated date of 22 April 2025 as the Mental Health Commission migrated to a new website platform and this was the date the page was developed. The Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensic Project is led by the North Metropolitan Health Service.
so_what: Confirms the Mental Health Commission page was frozen at Taskforce-era content because of a website migration, not neglect, and names North Metropolitan Health Service as the current project lead. Useful for redirecting scrutiny to the right accountable body — not evidence of anything being hidden.

topic: Taskforce meeting dates and staffing
question: I refer to Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensic Taskforce, and I ask: (a) On what dates have the taskforce met since 1 July 2024; (b) How many full-time equivalent roles support the taskforce; and (c) What are the titles of the roles under (b)?
answer_full:
(a) The Taskforce concluded its term in July 2023.

(b-c) N/A
so_what: Confirms the Taskforce ended mid-2023 and that no meeting-date or staffing questions apply after that, because the body no longer exists. Doesn't say who took over its functions, or through what governance structure decisions have been made since — that gap is now sharper, not smaller.

topic: CLMI Act 2023, demand modelling and Department of Justice involvement
question: I refer to the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 and the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project, and I ask: (a) What demand modelling has been done for forensic mental health beds in Western Australia, following the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 coming into force; (b) What risk assessments or analysis have been done to reflect the new legal framework for reintegration and community supervision orders created by the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023; (c) What involvement have the Department of Justice had with the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project; (d) What representations have the Department of Justice made to the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensic Taskforce; and (e) How has the community access model for patients at Graylands been changed by the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023?
answer_full:
(a) Demand modelling for statewide adult bed-based forensic mental health services in Western Australia was undertaken to support the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project, which included the anticipated impact of legislative changes of the Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 (CLMI Act).

(b) Analysis and assessment regarding legislative changes formed part of the whole-of-government implementation of the CLMI Act.

(c) The Department of Justice has been involved in the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project through interagency consultation and governance arrangements.

(d) The Department of Justice was represented in the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Taskforce until the Taskforce's term concluded in June 2023.

(e) The community access processes for CLMI-subject consumers remains largely consistent with the former Criminal Law Mentally Impaired Accused Act (1996) (WA).
so_what: The most substantive answer in the batch. Confirms demand modelling for extra forensic beds did factor in the CLMI Act, and that community access for this cohort remains largely consistent with the pre-2023 model — which corroborates, rather than contradicts, what this site has said about leave remaining a case-by-case decision. What it doesn't do: name the modelling, date it, or confirm it was ever tested against this specific site rather than statewide bed numbers. The government now admits the analysis exists. It still won't show it.

topic: IWA finding: further business cases and critical enablers
question: I refer to the quote "Further business cases will be developed to seek additional funding for various interdependent projects, with a number being critical enablers for this proposal." from Infrastructure WA's Major Infrastructure Proposal Assessment of the Graylands Hospital Redevelopment, and I ask: (a) Are further business cases being developed, as stated; (b) If yes to (a), what are these business cases being developed; (c) Which interdependent projects is Infrastructure WA referring to; (d) Which projects were deemed critical enablers for this proposal; and (e) Have funds been set aside for: (i) these various interdependent projects; and (ii) these further business cases?
answer_full:
(a)-(e) The State Government has engaged ADCO Constructions under the Early Contractor Involvement process to progress design for Stage 1 of the Graylands Campus Project. Future stages will be determined in due course.

Broader reconfiguration of WA mental health system involves reviewing current service delivery and identifying opportunities to support the evolving needs to the population. It includes evaluating demand, activity and capacity to inform future service and infrastructure planning, and engagement with key stakeholders to understand challenges and opportunities. The aim is to ensure service delivery is aligned with the strategic priorities and contemporary models of care.
so_what: Restates the Stage 1 contractor engagement and describes "broader reconfiguration" in general terms. Doesn't name a single one of the interdependent projects Infrastructure WA said were critical enablers for this one, or say whether any of them are funded.

topic: IWA finding: first of a series of investments
question: I refer to the quote "It is noted that the investment being sought is the first of a series of investments required for the broader reconfiguration of WA's mental health system." from Infrastructure WA's Major Infrastructure Proposal Assessment of the Graylands Hospital Redevelopment, and I ask: (a) What series of investments is Infrastructure WA referring to; (b) Which of the investments following the Graylands Hospital Redevelopment have since attracted funding; and (c) What does the broader reconfiguration of WA's mental health system entail?
answer_full:
(a-b) Please refer to LA QON 3084.

(c) Broader reconfiguration of WA mental health system involves reviewing current service delivery and identifying opportunities to support the evolving needs to the population. It includes evaluating demand, activity and capacity to inform future service and infrastructure planning, and engagement with key stakeholders to understand challenges and opportunities. The aim is to ensure service delivery is aligned with the strategic priorities and contemporary models of care.
so_what: Refers back to 3084 for funding detail and repeats the same general description of system-wide reconfiguration. Doesn't name what the "series of investments" Infrastructure WA referred to actually is — the true scale of what's been started is still undisclosed.

topic: IWA finding: business case had insufficient information
question: I refer to the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project and the quote "IWA considers that the business case on its own contains insufficient information on which to base an investment decision." from Infrastructure WA's Major Infrastructure Proposal Assessment of the Graylands Hospital Redevelopment, and I ask: (a) On what basis did the Minister make the investment decision; (b) Why was the business case considered insufficient; (c) What supplementary information was required to sufficiently base the investment decision; and (d) Was this supplementary information under (c) provided?
answer_full:
(a-d)

The future use of Graylands has been considered through extensive planning over more than a decade, including the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensic Taskforce established by the WA Government in 2021.

Following the Taskforce's recommendation to expand forensic mental health services on the northern portion of the site, further planning and design work led to the development of the Graylands Campus Project.
so_what: A direct, formal question — what did the Minister rely on, given Infrastructure WA said the business case was insufficient — got a non-answer: a decade of planning history and the 2021 Taskforce recommendation, with no mention of IWA's finding at all. This is now the single clearest example of the evidentiary gap this campaign has been pointing to: asked to explain the decision, the government describes the decision's history instead.

topic: Whether a Project Definition Plan exists
question: I refer to the Project Definition Plan for the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project, and I ask: (a) Is there a Project Definition Plan for the Graylands Reconfiguration and Forensics Project; (b) If yes to (a): (i) Where is this Project Definition Plan available; (ii) When was the Project Definition Plan created; and (iii) Does the Project Definition Plan outline how interdependent projects will be managed, as recommended by Infrastructure WA; and (c) If no to (a), why not?
answer_full:
(a-c)

The Cook Labor Government is delivering a record $5.5 billion health infrastructure program to significantly boost capacity across our health system.

As is the case for all major infrastructure projects, appropriate planning and due diligence is undertaken, including development of Project Definition Plans, to help inform delivery of the project.

As previously announced, the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre (CTRC) will be relocated to a new facility opposite the Graylands Hospital site to support the expansion. The State Government has allocated $10.6 million for the CTRC relocation.
so_what: Doesn't confirm whether a Project Definition Plan exists for this specific project, when it was made, or where it can be seen — despite this being a direct, simple question with a yes/no answer available. Talks instead about PDPs being standard practice generally. Combined with 3090, this is the clearest sign yet that formal parliamentary questions won't extract what FOI is now the only remaining route to get.

topic: Bed capacity by type, 2020–2029, across Graylands/Frankland/Selby
question: I refer to Graylands Hospital, the Frankland Centre, Selby Older Adult Mental Health Unit and the current program of works to the sites, and I ask: (a) Broken down by type of bed, how many beds did each of Graylands Hospital, the Frankland Centre and Selby Older Adult Mental Health Unit have capacity for, or is expected to have capacity for, at: (i) 30 June 2020; (ii) 30 June 2021; (iii) 30 June 2022; (iv) 30 June 2023; (v) 30 June 2024; (vi) 30 June 2025; (vii) 30 June 2026; (viii) 30 June 2027; (ix) 30 June 2028; and (x) 30 June 2029; and (b) For each type of bed under (a), how many such patients existed in Western Australia at each date (a)(i)–(x)?
answer_full:

It shows Stage 1 doesn't reduce today's general bed numbers at all (acute psychiatric actually rises to 67 and holds there through 2029) — the "zero general beds" long-term outcome depends entirely on a Stage 2 that, per 3084, remains unannounced and unfunded. Also gives the first public occupancy figures through 2026. Doesn't touch statewide unmet demand, which is a different question this campaign should keep asking.

topic: Campus security protocols, current and post-project
question: I refer to security at the Graylands Campus, and I ask: (a) What are the current security protocols of the Graylands Campus; (b) How are the security protocols adapting during the course of the Graylands Campus Project; and (c) What permanent security upgrades will be implemented as a result of the Graylands Campus Project?
answer_full:
(a-c)

Graylands Hospital is a fully authorised mental health inpatient facility that has existed in Mount Claremont for over a century.

In order to be authorised, a hospital or mental health ward must meet a series of stringent standards, including appropriate security protocols.

The expansion of Graylands Campus will continue to meet these standards.
so_what: Asked what current security protocols are, how they adapt during construction, and what permanent upgrades the campus will carry, the government said only that Graylands is authorised and will remain so. None of the three things asked were actually described. This is now the cleanest example on record of a direct, formal question producing zero operational detail — worth citing precisely because of how formal the opportunity to answer was.

topic: Dryandra Ward CLMI numbers vs Frankland Centre security
question: I refer to the Dryandra Ward of the State Forensic Mental Health Service, and I ask: (a) On 11 August 2026, how many consumers were subject to Criminal Law Mental Impairment (CLMI) custody orders; and (b) How does the security of the Dryandra Ward compare to the Frankland Centre?
answer_full:
(a) 13.

(b) Both the Frankland Centre and Dryandra Ward form part of the Graylands Hospital. Graylands Hospital is a fully authorised mental health inpatient facility that has existed in Mount Claremont for over a century. In order to be authorised, a hospital or mental health ward must meet a series of stringent standards, including appropriate security protocols.
so_what: Confirms 13 of Dryandra's 15 beds held CLMI custody-order patients on 11 August 2026 — a hard, current occupancy figure. The security comparison against Frankland that was actually asked for wasn't answered; the government repeated the same generic "authorised facility" line used for 3094.

topic: Risk-of-offending determination and ministerial engagement
question: I refer to the State Forensic Mental Health Service's provision of care for those at risk of serious offending as detailed on the North Metropolitan Health Service website, and I ask: (a) How is the risk of serious offending determined; and (b) What engagement has the Minister for Preventative Health had with the State Forensic Mental Health Service?
answer_full:
(a) The court makes a determination regarding risk of offending or other matters within the legal framework.

(b) The North Metropolitan Health Service has reported to the current Minister in her capacity as Minister for Health and Mental Health since March 2025.
so_what: A short answer that says more than it seems to: risk of offending is determined by the court, not by an independent clinical or security risk assessment process. That's close to confirming, in the government's own words, that no separate published risk assessment exists at the service level — which is exactly this campaign's central ask.

topic: Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre relocation — timing and cost
question: I refer to the relocation of the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre, and I ask: (a) When is the relocation expected to be complete; (b) What expenditure for the relocation will be required in 2027-28; (c) What works on the rest of the Graylands Campus will be undertaken concurrently with the relocation; and (d) What works on the rest of the Graylands Campus are contingent on the completion of the relocation?
answer_full:
(a-b) As previously announced, the State Government allocated $10.6 million in 2026-27 to relocate the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre and this is expected to be completed in mid-2027.

(c-d) Main works on the Graylands Campus Project are expected to follow the relocation.
so_what: Puts a hard date on the ground for the first time: CTRC relocation targeted for mid-2027, with the campus's main works expected to follow it. That's the clearest planning window available for pressing the government on consultation and disclosure before the next real construction decision — not a deadline to relax before.

topic: Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre relocation — funding and mitigation
question: I refer to the relocation of the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre, and I ask: (a) How is the Minister mitigating the impact of the relocation of the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre on preventative health; and (b) What funding does the Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre receive from the preventative health portfolio?
answer_full:
(a) The Cook Government is proud to be delivering its 2025 election commitment and has allocated $10.6 million to relocate Claremont Therapeutic Riding Centre to ensure it can continue operating and provide therapeutic support to its current and future clients.

(b) The service is a registered charity and receives funding through a variety of mechanisms including government agencies such as Lottery West, the Department of Local Government, Sport and Cultural Industries and Department of Communities.
so_what: Confirms the $10.6M relocation cost and that CTRC funding comes from Lotterywest, local government and community-services grants — not the preventative health portfolio the original question was fishing for a link to. Lower priority; mostly closes off a minor angle rather than opening one.

topic: Frankland Centre and Dryandra Ward occupancy, 2021–2025
question: I refer to the 30-bed Frankland Forensic Centre and the 15-bed Dryandra Ward, and I ask: (a) What was the occupancy rate for each centre for each of the following years: (i) 2021; (ii) 2022; (iii) 2023; (iv) 2024; and (v) 2025 to date?
answer_summary: Frankland Centre ran at 94–97% occupancy every year from 2021 to 2025 (30 operational beds throughout). Dryandra Ward's governance transferred to the State Forensic Mental Health Service on 31 July 2023; from that date its occupancy ran 66–76% against 8.7–12.2 average operational beds (of a 15-bed capacity). The answer notes forensic consumers under CLMI Act 2023 Custody Orders may have legally mandated overnight leave for up to 13 of 14 nights, which affects how occupancy is recorded.
so_what: Establishes that WA's existing forensic capacity has run near-full for five years — the demand case for more beds. It also shows occupancy figures are affected by legally mandated overnight leave, which is what community access under CLMI looks like in practice, and which — checked against the 1996 Act's own leave-of-absence provisions — is not a new feature: the 1996 Act capped leave orders at the same 14 days the current figures reference. That specific mechanism isn't new; the review structure around it is.

topic: People needing forensic mental health care held in prison instead
question: Since the commencement of WA's new Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 in September 2024, how many people with a mental impairment deemed suitable for care in a forensic facility are currently incarcerated in the WA prison system?
answer_summary: 15 people deemed suitable for care in a forensic mental health facility were, at the time of answering, held in the WA prison system instead — a direct capacity/demand data point.
so_what: A direct measure of unmet demand: people assessed as needing forensic mental health care were being held in prison instead. It is among the strongest public arguments for building more capacity, which this campaign does not dispute.

topic: Companion question to QoN 942
question: Since the commencement of WA's new Criminal Law (Mental Impairment) Act 2023 in September 2024, how many people with a mental impairment deemed suitable for care in a forensic facility are currently incarcerated in the WA prison system?
answer_summary: The Minister's written answer referred back to the answer given for QoN 942 (see above): 15 people.
so_what: Confirms the same figure was given across two portfolios, so it stands on the parliamentary record rather than resting on a single Minister's answer.

topic: Security incident, Graylands Hospital, 27 May 2023
question: I refer to the escape of a patient from Graylands Hospital on 27th May 2023, and his subsequent threatening behaviour on the day, and I ask: (a) What were the security measures at the Hospital for involuntary patients as at 27 May 2023; (b) How did the patient bypass those security measures; (c) How long was he gone from Graylands Hospital before his disappearance was noticed; and (d) What changes have been made to the security measures and monitoring systems at the Hospital since 27 May 2023 to: (i) prevent the escape of involuntary patients; and (ii) identify such an escape quickly and report to police immediately?
answer_summary: Asked in the 41st Parliament, before Sandra Brewer's or Libby Mettam's terms. The Minister's answer disputes the framing outright: “It is not correct to characterise the events the Member has referred to as an ‘escape’.” It states security measures for involuntary patients (who are not remanded or sentenced prisoners, on a Hospital Order, or under the Criminal Law (Mentally Impaired Accused) Act 1996) are assessed individually, and that policies and staff guidance on patient access to the Graylands Hospital grounds were under review as of the answer date. Distinct from the 2014 David Charles Batty incident already in the evidence pack.
so_what: The only public account of the 27 May 2023 incident, including how a departure from the site was characterised and recorded, and what changed afterwards.

topic: Mental health patient absconders by facility, 2012–13
question: I refer to Department of Health figures obtained through a freedom of information application that show 240 mental health patients were reported as absconders by staff in 2012–13 and I ask, which facilities did these patients abscond from and how many absconded from each facility?
answer_summary: Full facility breakdown provided; Graylands Hospital 153 of the state total of 240 (64%). Minister's answer defines ‘absconding’ broadly, including approved leave not returned by a specified time.
answer_full:
The definition of absconding is broad; for example, it includes patients who may be approved leave from inpatient care but have not returned to the ward by a specified time.

Hospitals:
Albany Hospital — 6
Armadale Hospital — fewer than 5
Bentley Adolescent Hospital — 22
Bentley Hospital — fewer than 5
Frankland Centre — fewer than 5
Graylands Hospital — 153
Joondalup Hospital — fewer than 5
Kalgoorlie Hospital — fewer than 5
Katanning Hospital — fewer than 5
Nickol Bay Hospital — fewer than 5
Peel Rockingham Kwinana Hospital — fewer than 5
Princess Margaret Hospital — 6
Royal Perth Hospital — 7
Swan Hospital — 13

Emergency Departments:
Albany Hospital — fewer than 5
Fremantle Hospital — fewer than 5
Geraldton Hospital — fewer than 5
Peel Rockingham Kwinana Hospital — fewer than 5
Port Hedland Hospital — fewer than 5
Royal Perth Hospital — fewer than 5

Other:

so_what: Graylands' general wards accounted for 153 of the 240 absconders reported statewide that year — but the same answer separately records Frankland Centre, the hospital's existing secure forensic unit, at fewer than 5. The 153 figure describes the general wards being demolished for Stage 1, not the forensic unit. That's a more precise, more defensible point than the headline number alone: it's the closer comparison for the new lower-security sub-acute unit, not for Frankland's own record.

topic: Assaults on nurses by facility, 2008–09
question: How many nurses have been assaulted by patients from 1 July 2008 – 30 June 2009 at each of Royal Perth, Sir Charles Gairdner, Fremantle, Osborne Park, Joondalup and Graylands Hospitals; what was the nature of each assault; and how many assaults toward nurses occurred at each Metropolitan Health Service hospital in 2008–09?
answer_summary: Graylands Hospital recorded 386 incidents, the highest of any metropolitan hospital — more than double the next-highest (Royal Perth, 163). Figures include verbal assault except at Sir Charles Gairdner. Nature of assaults recorded includes punching, kicking, biting, scratching, weapon use and stabbing with an object.
so_what: The only published hospital-by-hospital comparison of recorded incidents across metropolitan Perth. It dates from the general psychiatric era and the figures include verbal incidents, so it describes the site's history rather than the proposed forensic model.

topic: Current referral numbers and Frankland/Dryandra bed occupancy
question: I refer to the admitted services of the State Forensic Mental Health Service. (1) How many people are currently under referral to the State Forensic Mental Health Service by the courts and prisons via hospital and custody orders under the Criminal Law (Mentally Impairment) Act 2023 or under the Mental Health Act 2014? (2) On August 11, how many patients were being cared for at: (a) the Frankland Centre; and (b) the Dryandra Centre?
answer_summary: Answered the same sitting day by Hon Dr Katrina Stratton on behalf of the Minister for Health — this was a Question Without Notice (asked orally, with informal advance notice to the Minister's office), not a written Question on Notice like the other entries here. (1) 24 people currently under referral to the State Forensic Mental Health Service via hospital or custody orders. (2)(a) Frankland Centre: 30 patients — its full 30-bed capacity. (b) Dryandra: 14 patients, of 15-bed capacity. Snapshot as at 11 August 2026, two days after Sandra Brewer's written questions on this project were lodged.
so_what: A same-day snapshot showing the Frankland Centre at full capacity and Dryandra close to it, two days after the written questions on this project were lodged. It confirms current pressure on existing forensic beds from an independent source.
